findings.description: The RDS MySQL instance sets publicly_accessible = true, giving it an internet-routable endpoint (and its DNS is exported via the db_endpoint output). A backend datastore should only be reachable from within the VPC; this exposes MySQL to credential-guessing and exploitation from untrusted networks.
storage_encrypted = false disables KMS encryption of the RDS storage volume, snapshots and backups, leaving stored data unprotected at the storage layer.

The master username is the well-known value 'admin' and the password comes from a plain Terraform variable (persisted in cleartext in state and reused in EC2 user data) rather than Secrets Manager or a managed master password. Combined with public accessibility this makes brute-force or credential-leak attacks against a known account viable.

The attached parameter group sets no require_secure_transport (or equivalent SSL enforcement) and the application connects via plain mysqli_connect, so credentials and query data can traverse the network in cleartext — significant given the instance has a public endpoint.

The user_data script interpolates the database master username and var.password in cleartext into /var/www/inc/dbinfo.inc. User data is readable from the instance metadata service by any local process or SSRF vector, is retrievable via the EC2 API, and is stored in Terraform state.

No metadata_options block enforcing http_tokens = "required" is set, so IMDSv1 remains enabled. An SSRF in the PHP application would allow theft of the highly privileged ec2role instance-profile credentials and the plaintext user-data secrets.
No root_block_device with encrypted = true is specified, so the volume storing the plaintext dbinfo.inc credential file may be created unencrypted (unless account-level EBS default encryption is on).

The inline policy grants s3:*, ec2:* and rds:* on Resource "*" to the instance profile of an internet-facing web server. Compromise of the PHP application (e.g. via IMDSv1 credential theft) yields near-full control of S3 data, EC2 infrastructure (including ec2:RunInstances/PassRole-style escalation paths) and every RDS database in the account.
The database security group allows all protocols and ports outbound to 0.0.0.0/0, providing an unconstrained channel for data exfiltration or command-and-control from the data tier.

The security group intended to segment the RDS instance carries only a VPC-CIDR ingress rule plus a wide-open egress rule, and the database itself is publicly_accessible = true, so the group provides no meaningful boundary for the data tier. (The reviewers' 'missing description' point is stylistic; the substantive issue is the weak boundary.)
